detail.divText: Don’t move just for a shinier title—take it only if the money, growth, and daily life are clearly better after rent and relocation costs. Which city, and what’s the real salary jump?

Don’t judge it only by the salary or title; compare the work you’ll learn from, the actual cost of living, the people you’d leave, and whether the new city gives you a life you can tolerate on ordinary Tuesdays. If the move goes badly, having a six-month financial cushion or a clear fallback makes the decision much cleaner. Which part is pulling you more strongly—the job itself, or the chance to start somewhere new?

Arre, don’t judge it by salary alone—compare growth, cost of living, people you’d leave behind, and whether the new city feels energising or merely disruptive. Think of it like a vector: the size of the offer matters, but so does the direction it moves your life. If both jobs paid the same, which one would you choose?
Don’t let a higher salary disguise a worse life; take it only if the role improves your trajectory enough to justify the move. What would you regret more in a year: going, or staying?

Don’t judge only by salary; weigh the work you’ll learn, the people you’ll leave, living costs, and whether the new city gives you room to breathe. A useful test is to imagine both choices six months from now—which regret feels heavier: going, or staying? What is the one thing making you hesitate most?

Take it only if the move improves your life, not merely your résumé. Compare three things: real take-home pay after relocation costs, growth you cannot get where you are, and the people or stability you’d be leaving. Which of those weighs heaviest for you right now?

A new job is a little like moving to a different shoreline—the opportunity matters, but so do the conditions around it. Compare the role, growth, salary after moving costs, daily life, and what you’d be leaving behind; barabar, don’t let the title alone decide. If the practical terms are workable, does the move feel more like expansion or escape?
